L.D. 476: An Act to Ban the Sale of Polystyrene Packing Peanuts in the State Testimony of: Carla Hopkins, Director, Division of Materials Management, DEP Public Hearing: March 3, 2025
Page 2 of 3
Chapter 15-A) prohibits the use of single use disposable polystyrene foam food service containers by food establishments. lt does not, however, ban the actual sale of
polystyrene foam food containers. For example, a non-food establishment may sell
polystyrene foam food containers for personal use. L.D. 476 takes the opposite approach to minimizing the use of polystyrene foam by banning the sale of loose polystyrene packing materials, also known as packing peanuts, instead of banning the use of these items. This means that while these items cannot be sold in Maine, they can still be used or brought into Maine. Where Title 38 Chapter 15-A and L.D. 476 both address minimizing polystyrene foam in different products in very different ways, it is
anticipated that there will be confusion as to how these different products fall under very
different restrictions regarding their sales and use.
Additionally, the wording of L.D. 476 does not clearly limit the sales ban to only packing
peanuts as the bill summary would indicate. The language of the bill, whether
intentional or not, could be interpreted to include all types and sizes of polystyrene packing material, including sheets and blocks of polystyrene foam used for shipping large, expensive, fragile items and polystyrene foam that is a component of shipping
protection material that contains other material.
Finally, the language of the bill as proposed would not prohibit the distribution of products packaged using polystyrene foam into the state, nor would it prevent Maine businesses from using polystyrene foam that is purchased from another state or that already exists. Both of these scenarios identify that there would still be a need for Maine businesses, municipalities and consumers to handle and dispose of these packing materials. Since this ban applies to sales of polystyrene foam, Maine businesses will
not be allowed to purchase polystyrene foam in Maine which may put Maine businesses at a competitive disadvantage to out-of-state businesses who may still purchase this
material in their states at lower cost.

Additionally, it should be noted that passage of this proposed bill would require a fiscal note, as additional Department resources would be required to enforce this sales ban as well as to provide educational resources as to what the sales ban does and does not
include.
Thank you for the opportunity to testify before you today. I would be happy to answer any questions from the Committee, both now and at the work session.

Testimony of Senator Denise Tepler introducing L.D. 476 An Act to Ban the Sale
Polystyrene Peanuts in the State Before the Joint Standing Committee on Enviornment and Natural Resources
March 03, 2025 Representative Doudera and distinguished colleagues of the Enviromnent and Natural Resources
Committee,
I am Senator Denise Tepler, representing Senate District 24, all of Sagadahoc County and the Town of Dresden, and a long-time resident of Topsham. I am here today to introduce L.D. 476,
"An Act to Ban the Sale of Polystyrene Peanuts in the State."
As many of you may know, in addition to serving on this committee, I co-chair the Marine Resources Committee (MAR). There are several reasons I care deeply about this bill. As the experts who testify after me will no doubt share with you, styrene is poisonous to both htnnans and fish. And Expanded Polystyrene, which we know as Styrofoam, is one of the most common forms of plastic pollution in our oceans. The small pieces of styrofoam which we use as packing material are light and easily blown out of landfills. They make their way to the water where they
float and are sometimes mistaken as food by sea animals.
We are trying in MAR to preserve the traditional livelihood of men and women in coastal Maine
-- fishing in all its forms -- and to make certain that the next generation will find lobsters and ocean fin fish to catch. We know that our near ocean is changing rapidly. It is warming quickly
and water quality is diminishing. I want to do everything I can to keep Maine's iconic coastlines and ocean waters as clear and beautiful as possible for all our children and grandchildren.
Banning more forms of toxic polystyrene in addition to food containers which are bamed now, is
a part of that effort.
A personal experience about 8 years ago also influenced my decision to support this effort. My
family and I traveled to Ambergris Caye, an island off the coast of Belize, for a sun and sand
beach vacation. Unfortunately, a "recycling" scow just off the coast had dumped it's load a few days before we arrived and the beaches up and down the island, except at several resorts where they had cleaned them, were strewn with crushed plastic garbage of many kinds but especially
polystyrene -- which got stuck in the mangroves and reeds along the shore as well as sitting in piles on the narrow beaches. It was an apocalyptic view of the future, if we don't work hard to
limit the plastics that linger in our environment.
Please join me in voting to ban expanded polystyrene packing pieces to protect our oceans and
marine animals, our fishing industry, and the beauty of shorelines here and elsewhere.

To:  Joint Standing Committee on Environment and Natural Resources From: Elizabeth Schwartz, Sierra Club Maine Volunteer Date:  March 3, 2025
Re:  Testimony in Support of L.D. 476: An Act to Ban the Sale of Polystyrene Packing Peanuts in the State
Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera, and members of the Joint Committee on Environment and Natural Resources,
I am testifying on behalf of Sierra Club Maine, representing over 22,000 supporters and members statewide. Founded in 1892, Sierra Club is one of our nation's oldest and largest environmental organizations. We work diligently to amplify the power of our 3.8 million members and supporters nation-wide. In keeping with our mission to reduce pollution and our use of unnecessary petroleum products, we urge you to support the end of the sale of polystyrene packing peanuts in Maine through L.D. 476.
This bill prohibits the sale or offer to sell "loose polystyrene packing material," commonly known as foam packing peanuts. Polystyrene packing peanuts are made from expanded polystyrene, which is a type of plastic manufactured from petroleum-based chemicals and other synthetic additives.
Expanded polystyrene does not readily biodegrade, rather it breaks up into smaller and smaller pieces due to its brittle texture. As expanded polystyrene breaks up into tiny pieces, the pieces quickly disperse into the environment and spread in the air and water, and can be mistaken for food by animals. Despite this product often being used for single use, it has a lasting environmental impact.
In addition to not biodegrading, polystyrene is incredibly difficult to recycle. EcoMaine, the recycling company that services one third of the state, does not recycle packing peanuts in their facility, as the closest foam recycling facility is in New Jersey. With one percent or less of plastic foam waste being recycled in the United States per year, this is a product that must be banned. Especially with a plethora of affordable alternatives already on the market. Large companies like FedEx, have not used them in locations nationwide in several years, and most UPS Store locations in Maine have also stopped using them already.
In 2012, scientists examining a dead leatherback sea turtle (vulnerable) in Maine found that plastic in its gastrointestinal tract potentially contributed to its death. Expanded polystyrene is one of the most abundant types of plastic pollution found in U.S. rivers, lakes, and marine

environments. Maine depends on clean waterways and coastlines to support 60,000 American jobs and $3.8 billion in GDP in our coastal tourism, fishing, and recreation industries. All of that is put at risk by the staggering amount of plastic entering our oceans and other waterways.
Many other states have already passed foam packing peanut bans including, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, California, and the District of Columbia. A recent poll by Oceana shows strong public support for reducing plastic waste. This poll found that 81% of U.S. voters support reducing the amount of plastic that is produced and 80% of U.S. voters support state and local policies that reduce single-use plastic foam. This data shows that there is a widespread concern about the environmental impact of these materials in our communities. Additionally, 82% of U.S. voters support reducing the amount of single-use plastic state and federal governments buy and use. These numbers show that a large majority of Americans are eager to see legislative action that prioritizes sustainability, human health, and protection of our waterways.
We encourage the committee to support L.D. 476 and help move Maine towards a cleaner, more pollution-free future.
Elizabeth Schwartz Sierra Club Maine Chapter Volunteer

To: Senator Denise Tepler, Presenter and Chair of the Committee On Environment and Natural Resources, and the other Honorable members of the Committee On Environment and Natural Resources
Regarding: Testimony in support of LD 476, An Act to Ban the Sale of Polystyrene Packing Peanuts in the State
My name is Luke Valleli, and I am a Maine voter and student at the University of Maine. I am writing to voice my support of LD 476. While I unfortunately imagine that this act may seem trivial and silly to some Mainers and members of our Legislature, it embodies key traits of the Mainer spirit: love and dedication for our environment and natural resources, consideration for our fellow Mainers, and putting real, everyday interests ahead of pinching pennies that line corporate pocketbooks. Packing peanuts break apart and leach without decomposing, thus polluting Maine's beloved lands and waters, damaging wildlife, and harming residents of the state. Littered polystyrene packing materials are associated in particular with threats to marine life, which is of particular concern. Maine is home to endangered fish such as the Atlantic Salmon and Shortnose Sturgeon, and these fish certainly contribute to the immense value of Maine's biodiversity. Furthermore, biodegradable and renewable packing alternatives such as crumpled paper can further act to buoy Maine's longstanding timber and pulp and paper industries.
Respectfully submitted,
Luke Valleli

Surfrider Maine Public Testimony in Support of LD 476 - An Act to Ban the Sale of Polystyrene Packing Peanuts in the State
Presented by Mariel Geiger, Climate Action Chair and Policy Lead Surfrider Foundation Maine Chapter
Dear Members of the ENR Committee, Senator Tepler & Representative Doudera,
Good morning! My name is Mariel Geiger, and I'm here today representing the Surfrider Foundation Maine Chapter, where I serve as Climate Action Chair and Policy Lead. On behalf of Surfrider and our network of coastal advocates, I urge you to support this important measure to prohibit the sale of loose polystyrene packing materials, commonly known as packing peanuts, here in Maine.
Surfrider is a national ocean conservation foundation comprised of a network of chapters in coastal states and here in Maine we have a very dedicated boots on the ground team and we frequently find polystyrene foam and broken-down particles littering our beaches, salt marshes, and riverbanks.
We know that polystyrene is one of the most persistent and harmful types of plastic pollution. Because it breaks apart so easily into small pieces, which are extremely difficult to remove once they enter the environment. And honestly -- if you've ever opened a box filled with packing peanuts, you already know they're a menace. They stick to everything and if you've ever tried to chase down a rogue packing peanut blowing across your driveway, you already know how stubborn they can be. Now imagine trying to gather them off a windy beach or out of a tidal marsh.
We believe that it's important to focus on products themselves but also the entire life of that material and it's impacts. So always keeping in mind the waste of something used for such a short period of time and the toxicity of that waste in the environment, but then also circling back to the toxicity of production and those impacts on human health and of course the resourcing, resource depletion and again the toxic elements of that process. Another very compelling factor that we consider is that packaging waste is now the largest contributor to plastic pollution globally.

Eliminating the sale of polystyrene peanuts is a simple and commonsense next step to reduce this harmful pollution throughout Maine's iconic coastline, marine habitats, fisheries and environment in general. And from all of our advocates here at Surfrider Maine we would urge you to support this measure and we appreciate that you are keeping Maine on the right track continuing to lead on plastic pollution reduction and ensuring a cleaner and safer environment for everyone.
Mariel Geiger | Maine Chapter Climate Action Chair and Policy Lead Surfrider Foundation Maine Chapter | climate@maine.surfrider.org
